claim: GGN is a unique giant GABAergic neuron that plays a central role in structuring olfactory codes in the locust mushroom body.
source: GGN, a unique giant GABAergic neuron that plays a central role in structuring olfactory codes in the locust mushroom body.
evidence: This is a characterization of GGN based on established knowledge about this neuron in the locust.

claim: Depolarizing GGN at its input branch can globally inhibit KCs several hundred microns away.
source: Our simulations suggest that depolarizing GGN at its input branch can globally inhibit KCs several hundred microns away.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational simulations described in the manuscript.

claim: GGN responds to odors with complex temporal patterns of depolarization and hyperpolarization that can vary with odors and across animals.
source: Our in vivorecordings show that GGN responds to odors with complex temporal patterns of depolarization and hyperpolarization that can vary with odors and across animals
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo electrophysiological recordings presented in the manuscript.

claim: The model predicts the existence of a yet-undiscovered olfactory pathway.
source: leading our model to predict the existence of a yet-undiscovered olfactory pathway.
evidence: This is a prediction based on computational modeling results.

claim: Multiple types of olfactory receptor neurons can respond to a given odor with vigorous bursts of action potentials.
source: Multiple types of olfactory receptor neurons can respond to a given odor with vigorous bursts of action potentials
evidence: This is established knowledge about olfactory receptor neuron responses.

claim: Neurons in the pyriform cortex (vertebrates) or mushroom body (insects) respond to odors with only a spike or two.
source: while neurons deeper in the brain, in the pyriform cortex (vertebrates) or mushroom body (insects), respond to the same odor with only a spike or two (Laurent and Naraghi, 1994b; Friedrich and Laurent, 2001; Perez-Orive et al., 2002; Cang and Isaacson, 2003; Bathellier et al., 2008; Poo and Isaacson, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: Information about odors in higher order neurons is represented sparsely by the identities of the active neurons (population coding) and in the timing of the few spikes elicited in those neurons (temporal coding).
source: In these higher order neurons, information about odors is represented sparsely by the identities of the active neurons (population coding) and in the timing of the few spikes elicited in those neurons (temporal coding) (Perez-Orive et al., 2002; Poo and Isaacson, 2009; Stettler and Axel, 2009; Gupta and Stopfer, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: In both vertebrates and invertebrates multiple mechanisms interact to mediate olfactory transformations, including important inhibitory contributions from GABAergic neurons.
source: In both vertebrates and invertebrates multiple mechanisms interact to mediate these transformations, including important inhibitory contributions from GABAergic neurons (Luna and Pettit, 2010; Papadopoulou et al., 2011; Lin et al., 2014; Palmer and Harvey, 2014; Large et al., 2016; Large et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: In the absence of environmental odors, olfactory receptor neurons (ORNs) in the locust antenna are spontaneously active.
source: In the absence of environmental odors, olfactory receptor neurons (ORNs) in the antenna are spontaneously active.
evidence: This is established knowledge about locust ORN activity.

claim: Odorants elicit increases or decreases in the spontaneous firing rates of ORNs.
source: Odorants elicit increases or decreases in the spontaneous firing rates of ORNs
evidence: This is established knowledge about ORN responses to odorants.

claim: Spontaneous activity in ORNs drives background spiking in PNs.
source: Spontaneous activity in ORNs drives background spiking in PNs (Joseph et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: PNs respond to odor-evoked responses in ORNs with sometimes-elaborate firing patterns that are further shaped by inhibition from the antennal lobe's local interneurons (LNs).
source: PNs respond to the variety of odor-evoked responses in ORNs with sometimes-elaborate firing patterns that are further shaped by inhibition from the antennal lobe's local interneurons (LNs) (Raman et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Spikes in PNs are coaxed into rhythmic waves by fast reciprocal interactions between excitatory PNs and inhibitory LNs.
source: Spikes in PNs are also coaxed into rhythmic waves by fast reciprocal interactions between excitatory PNs and inhibitory LNs (MacLeod and Laurent, 1996; Bazhenov et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Odor-elicited firing patterns distributed across the population of PNs are informative about the identity, concentration, and timing of the odor.
source: Odor-elicited firing patterns distributed across the population of PNs are informative about the identity, concentration, and timing of the odor (Laurent et al., 1996; Stopfer et al., 2003; Brown et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: KCs are nearly silent at rest and respond very selectively to odors by generating very few spikes.
source: Unlike the volubly spiking PNs, KCs are nearly silent at rest and respond very selectively to odors by generating very few spikes (Laurent and Naraghi, 1994b; Perez-Orive et al., 2002; Joseph et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Any given odor evokes responses in a small fraction of the KC population, and any KC responds to a small set of odors.
source: Thus, any given odor evokes responses in a small fraction of the KC population, and any KC responds to a small set of odors (Perez-Orive et al., 2002; Stopfer et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: Sparseness of activity in KCs is thought to arise mainly from specialized membrane conductances that amplify only strong, synchronized input and a feedback circuit that tamps down their spiking with cyclic inhibition.
source: This sparseness of activity in KCs is thought to arise mainly from two factors: specialized membrane conductances that amplify only strong, synchronized input; and a feedback circuit that tamps down their spiking with cyclic inhibition (Perez-Orive et al., 2002; Demmer and Kloppenburg, 2009; Papadopoulou et al., 2011; Lin et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: In the locust the main sources of inhibition to KCs are the giant GABAergic neurons (GGNs), one on each side of the brain.
source: In the locust the main sources of this inhibition are the giant GABAergic neurons (GGNs), one on each side of the brain (Leitch and Laurent, 1996; Papadopoulou et al., 2011; Gupta and Stopfer, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: GGN is reported to receive excitatory input from all 50,000 KCs at synapses within the mushroom body's α lobe.
source: It is reported to receive excitatory input from all 50,000 KCs at synapses within the mushroom body's α lobe
evidence: This is a reported characteristic of GGN connectivity.

claim: GGN provides inhibitory feedback to all KCs 400–500 μm away within the calyx.
source: and, in turn, provide inhibitory feedback to all KCs 400–500 μm away within the calyx.
evidence: This is a reported characteristic of GGN function.

claim: GGN receives inhibitory input from a spiking neuron named 'Inhibitor of GGN' (IG) which itself receives inhibition from GGN.
source: In addition, GGN receives inhibitory input from a spiking neuron aptly named 'Inhibitor of GGN' (IG) which itself receives inhibition from GGN (Figure 1a, right) (Papadopoulou et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and reference to Figure 1a.

claim: GGN is a non-spiking interneuron.
source: GGN is a non-spiking interneuron.
evidence: This is an established characteristic of GGN.

claim: Odor presentations, spiking in KCs, and intracellular current injections depolarize GGN, but none of these stimuli causes GGN to generate spikes.
source: Odor presentations, spiking in KCs, and intracellular current injections have all been shown to depolarize GGN, but none of these stimuli causes GGN to generate spikes; even strong intracellular current injections into GGN elicit only passive responses (Leitch and Laurent, 1996; Papadopoulou et al., 2011); and our own observations).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and the authors' own observations.

claim: GGN has very thin, feather-like neurites that wrap around and penetrate the peduncle of the mushroom body.
source: We further observed, for the first time, myriad thin fibers that emerge from the stems of the calyceal branches, splitting into very fine feather-like neurites that wrap densely around the peduncle, with some investing the peduncle core (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is a novel observation made by the authors and shown in Figure 1b.

claim: GGN's neurites in the calyx and lateral horn are dotted with many irregular bouton-like structures.
source: The neurites in the calyx and lateral horn are dotted with many irregular bouton-like structures (Figure 1c)
evidence: This observation is supported by Figure 1c.

claim: The maximum path length of GGN's neuronal trees is on the order of 2 mm.
source: Analyzing these traces, we found that the maximum path length of the neuronal trees (i.e., the maximum distance between any two points on the neuronal tree when traversed along the neurites) was on the order of 2 mm
evidence: This is a measurement from the morphological reconstruction.

claim: The maximum physical length of GGN is on the order of 1 mm.
source: and the maximum physical length (i.e., Euclidean distance between any two points on the neuron in three-dimensions) was on the order of 1 mm.
evidence: This is a measurement from the morphological reconstruction.

claim: Some neurites of GGN at their thickest were nearly 20 μm in diameter.
source: Some neurites at their thickest were nearly 20 μm in diameter.
evidence: This is a measurement from the morphological reconstruction.

claim: The total traced branch length of GGN was about 65 mm.
source: The total traced branch length (i.e., the sum of the lengths of all the neurites) was about 65 mm (although many vanishingly thin branches were too fine to trace).
evidence: This is a measurement from the morphological reconstruction.

claim: GGN fell into the 99.75th percentile for total branch length compared to 96,831 vertebrate and invertebrate neurons cataloged in the neuromorpho.org database.
source: Compared to 96,831 vertebrate and invertebrate neurons cataloged in the neuromorpho.org database, GGN fell into the 99.75th percentile for total branch length
evidence: This is a comparative analysis using data from neuromorpho.org.

claim: GGN fell into the 99.95th percentile for number of branch points compared to 96,831 vertebrate and invertebrate neurons cataloged in the neuromorpho.org database.
source: and the 99.95th percentile for number of branch points.
evidence: This is a comparative analysis using data from neuromorpho.org.

claim: Cable theory predicts that a passive voltage signal within GGN's structure will attenuate dramatically as it encounters cytosolic resistance along the neurites.
source: Cable theory applied to neurons (Rall, 1964) predicts that a passive voltage signal within such a structure will attenuate dramatically as it encounters cytosolic resistance along the neurites
evidence: This is a prediction based on established cable theory.

claim: Passive voltage signals in GGN will attenuate further as they divide at the neuronal arbor's branch points.
source: will attenuate further as it divides at the neuronal arbor's branch points
evidence: This is a prediction based on established cable theory.

claim: Passive voltage signals in GGN will leak out through ionic channels in the cell membrane.
source: and will leak out through ionic channels in the cell membrane.
evidence: This is a prediction based on established cable theory.

claim: GGN inhibits KCs.
source: It has been shown that GGN inhibits KCs (Papadopoulou et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published research.

claim: Prior studies in invertebrates have shown that 2–5 mV depolarizations in nonspiking interneurons suffice to evoke changes in the membrane potentials of their post-synaptic neurons.
source: Prior studies in invertebrates have shown that 2–5 mV depolarizations in nonspiking interneurons suffice to evoke changes in the membrane potentials of their post-synaptic neurons (Burrows and Siegler, 1978; Manor et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published research.

claim: The model showed that electrical signals undergo substantial attenuation as they travel through GGN.
source: Our model showed that, although electrical signals do undergo substantial attenuation as they travel through GGN
evidence: This is a result from the computational model.

claim: Signals arising in GGN's α lobe branches appear to remain strong enough to provide global inhibition to KCs in the calyx.
source: signals arising in its α lobe branches appear to remain strong enough to provide global inhibition to KCs in the calyx.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the computational model.

claim: In vivo recordings show GGN's membrane potential rests at about −51 mV.
source: In vivo, intracellular recordings (Papadopoulou et al., 2011; and our own) show GGN's membrane potential rests at about −51 mV.
evidence: This is supported by citations and the authors' own recordings.

claim: Strong odor stimuli depolarize GGN by about 10 mV in recordings made near the base of the α lobe branch.
source: Because strong odor stimuli depolarize GGN by about 10 mV in recordings made near the base of the α lobe branch (Papadopoulou et al., 2011) (also see Figure 4)
evidence: This is supported by a citation and reference to Figure 4.

claim: A 10 mV depolarization in GGN's α lobe branch yields depolarizations ranging from ~5–9 mV throughout the calyx.
source: Notably, the extent of signal attenuation was substantial and varied throughout the calyx, yielding depolarizations ranging from ~5–9 mV.
evidence: This is a result from the voltage clamp simulation shown in Figure 2.

claim: The signal decreased with branch distance from the α lobe, leaving the least amount of signal at the medial portion of the lateral calyceal branch.
source: The signal decreased with branch distance from the α lobe, leaving the least amount of signal at the medial portion of the lateral calyceal branch (Figure 2b,c, Figure 2—video 1).
evidence: This is a result from the simulation shown in Figure 2.

claim: Higher axial resistivity yields greater signal attenuation in GGN.
source: As expected, higher RA yielded greater signal attenuation
evidence: This is a result from parameter exploration in the model.

claim: Higher membrane resistivity yields less signal attenuation in GGN.
source: whereas higher RM yielded less signal attenuation (Figure 2g).
evidence: This is a result from parameter exploration shown in Figure 2g.

claim: Except for the most extreme values of the parameter range, signals from the α lobe remained strong enough throughout the calyx (>2–5 mV) to support synaptic transmission.
source: This analysis suggests that signal transmission in GGN is robust: except for the most extreme values of this parameter range, signals from the α lobe remained strong enough throughout the calyx (>2–5 mV) to support synaptic transmission.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the parameter exploration analysis.

claim: Feedback inhibition from GGN sparsens the odor-elicited responses of KCs by increasing the KC spiking threshold.
source: In vivo, feedback inhibition from GGN sparsens the odor-elicited responses of KCs by increasing the KC spiking threshold
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: Feedback inhibition from GGN restricts KC spiking to brief temporal windows defined by the oscillatory cycle established in the AL.
source: and by restricting KC spiking to brief temporal windows defined by the oscillatory cycle established in the AL (Papadopoulou et al., 2011; Gupta and Stopfer, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Large-scale feedforward inhibition has been shown to expand the dynamic range of cortical neurons.
source: Large-scale feedforward inhibition has previously been shown to expand the dynamic range of cortical neurons (Pouille et al., 2009)
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: In Drosophila, feedback inhibition from APL expands the dynamic range of KCs.
source: and in Drosophila, feedback inhibition from APL, the analog of GGN, expands the dynamic range of KCs (Inada et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: Baseline inhibition from spontaneous activity in GGN increased the KC's threshold for spiking.
source: As expected, baseline inhibition from spontaneous activity in GGN increased the KC's threshold for spiking.
evidence: This is a result from the model simulation shown in Figure 3.

claim: The GGN-coupled KC continued to spike over a much larger range of current injection than the isolated KC.
source: Notably, though, the GGN-coupled KC continued to spike over a much larger range of current injection than the isolated KC, which quickly saturated to a level where it could no longer spike (Figure 3b,c).
evidence: This is a result from the model simulation shown in Figure 3.

claim: Feedback inhibition from GGN allows an individual KC to function effectively over a larger dynamic range of inputs.
source: These results suggested that feedback inhibition from GGN allows an individual KC to function effectively over a larger dynamic range of inputs.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the model simulation.

claim: The model predicts that feedback inhibition from GGN expands the dynamic range of KCs.
source: Thus, our model predicts that feedback inhibition from GGN expands the dynamic range of KCs.
evidence: This is a prediction from the model.

claim: Recordings from GGN frequently revealed depolarizations throughout an odor presentation, often with stronger depolarizing peaks upon the odor's onset and offset.
source: Our recordings made in vivo from GGN frequently revealed depolarizations throughout an odor presentation, often with stronger depolarizing peaks upon the odor's onset and offset (Figure 4, Animal 1, hexanol) (see also Papadopoulou et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo recordings shown in Figure 4 and a citation.

claim: Recordings from GGN sometimes revealed more complex odor-elicited responses than previously reported, including combinations of depolarization and hyperpolarization.
source: Notably, though, our recordings from GGN sometimes revealed more complex odor-elicited responses than previously reported, including combinations of depolarization and hyperpolarization (Figure 4, Animal 1, hexanal).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo recordings shown in Figure 4.

claim: The same GGN could respond differently when different odors were presented.
source: Moreover, we found that the same GGN could respond differently when different odors were presented; for example, GGNs from Animals 2 and 3 shown in Figure 4 depolarized in response to one odor and hyperpolarized in response to another.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo recordings shown in Figure 4.

claim: GGNs in different animals could respond differently to the same odor.
source: Also, GGNs in different animals could respond differently to the same odor (Figure 4, hexanal).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo recordings shown in Figure 4.

claim: Almost a quarter of the odor-GGN pairs in in vivo recordings showed reliable hyperpolarizations at some point in the odor response.
source: Almost a quarter of the odor-GGN pairs in our in vivo recordings showed reliable hyperpolarizations at some point in the odor response (40 out of 169).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from in vivo recordings.

claim: Each model KC was connected to 50% of the 830 PN spike trains via excitatory synapses, following observations made in vivo.
source: To provide excitatory input to the KCs, the firing patterns of 830 PNs were simulated as spike-trains, and, following observations made in vivo (Jortner et al., 2007), each KC was stimulated by 50% of these spike trains via excitatory synapses.
evidence: This is a model design choice based on in vivo observations cited.

claim: 77% of the PN spike trains were assigned a spontaneous firing rate of 2.6 spikes/s.
source: Thus, 77% of the PN spike trains were assigned a spontaneous firing rate of 2.6 spikes/s
evidence: This is a parameter in the model based on PN firing statistics.

claim: During odor stimulation, 20% of spontaneously active PNs were switched to 20 spikes/s modulated by the 20 Hz oscillations generated in the antennal lobe.
source: during odor stimulation, 20% of these PNs were switched to 20 spikes/s modulated by the 20 Hz oscillations generated in the antennal lobe and reflected in the local field potential (LFP)
evidence: This is a parameter in the model based on PN firing statistics.

claim: During odor stimulation, 10% of spontaneously active PNs were inhibited (no spikes).
source: and 10% were inhibited (no spikes) (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is a parameter in the model shown in Figure 5b.

claim: A model with simplified, homogenous firing patterns in PNs and uniform synaptic strengths generates unrealistic membrane potential in GGN.
source: Simulations of this model produced a few highly synchronized bouts of spiking in the KC population (Figure 5c), and corresponding isolated peaks in GGN's membrane potential (Figure 5d).
evidence: This is a result from the model simulation shown in Figure 5.

claim: A model combining heterogeneous connectivity with structured PN firing patterns gave rise to GGN voltage traces that included sustained depolarization and temporal dynamics more characteristic of responses observed in vivo.
source: However, a model combining heterogeneous connectivity with structured PN firing patterns gave rise to GGN voltage traces that included sustained depolarization and temporal dynamics more characteristic of responses we had observed in vivo (Figure 5h,i).
evidence: This is a result from the model simulation shown in Figure 5.

claim: The distribution of firing rates of the KC population in simulations showed that, while most KCs produced 0–2 odor-elicited spikes, a few KCs spiked much more.
source: The distribution of firing rates of the KC population in our simulations showed that, while most KCs produced 0–2 odor-elicited spikes, a few KCs spiked much more (Figure 6a and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a result from the model simulation shown in Figure 6.

claim: The average spontaneous firing rates of KCs recorded in vivo were very low (~0.09 Hz).
source: On average, the spontaneous firing rates of these real KCs were very low (~0.09 Hz)
evidence: This is a result from patch clamp recordings from 147 KCs.

claim: KC firing rates reached only somewhat higher rates during odor presentation and immediately after odor termination (~0.15 and~0.16 Hz, respectively).
source: and reached only somewhat higher rates during odor presentation and immediately after odor termination (~0.15 and~0.16 Hz, respectively, Figure 6b), as previously observed (Perez-Orive et al., 2002; Gupta and Stopfer, 2014).
evidence: This is a result from patch clamp recordings shown in Figure 6b and supported by citations.

claim: The distribution of spike counts in KCs tested in vivo was clustered close to 0 but included a long rightward tail.
source: Overall, the distribution of spike counts in KCs we tested in vivo was clustered close to 0 but included a long rightward tail (Figure 6g), in agreement with our model (Figure 6a).
evidence: This is a result from in vivo recordings shown in Figure 6g.

claim: When KCs producing more than five odor-elicited spikes were removed from the model, a different set of KCs emerged to replace them by becoming more active.
source: We found that when KCs producing more than five odor-elicited spikes were removed (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), a different set of KCs emerged to replace them by becoming more active.
evidence: This is a result from the model simulation shown in Figure 7.

claim: The replacement high spike-rate KCs were fewer in number than the original high-firing set.
source: However, the replacement high spike-rate KCs were fewer in number than the original high-firing set (Figure 7a).
evidence: This is a result from the model simulation shown in Figure 7a.

claim: The high spike-rate KCs in the model are not a static population, but rather change in identity, reflecting emergent features of the network's distribution of synaptic conductances, PN input, and GGN feedback.
source: Our analysis showed two things: first, the high spike-rate KCs in our model are not a static population, but rather change in identity, reflecting emergent features of the network's distribution of synaptic conductances, PN input, and GGN feedback
evidence: This is a conclusion from the model analysis.

claim: High-spike rate KCs augment the depolarization of GGN to realistic levels.
source: and second, high-spike rate KCs augment the depolarization of GGN to realistic levels.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the model analysis.

claim: Intracellular recordings from GGN revealed extended periods of odor-elicited hyperpolarization.
source: Our intracellular recordings from GGN revealed extended periods of odor-elicited hyperpolarization (Figure 4), something not previously reported in recordings made in vivo nor explained by existing models of GGN within its olfactory network.
evidence: This is a result from in vivo recordings shown in Figure 4.

claim: A previous report showed spikes in IG correlate one-to-one with IPSPs in GGN.
source: However, a previous report showed spikes in IG correlate one-to-one with IPSPs in GGN (Papadopoulou et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: Recordings made in vivo from GGN revealed IPSPs in the absence of odors.
source: Our recordings made in vivo from GGN revealed IPSPs in the absence of odors
evidence: This is a result from in vivo recordings.

claim: Odor presentations caused the frequency of IPSPs in GGN to increase.
source: and that odor presentations caused the frequency of IPSPs to increase (Wilcoxon signed-rank test, N = 198 pairs, W = 2328.5, p<<0.001; responses from two animals are shown in Figure 8a, and responses from 1257 trials with several odors from 47 GGNs are shown as a peri-stimulus time histogram in Figure 8b and c.)
evidence: This is a result from in vivo recordings shown in Figure 8 with statistical analysis.

claim: IG's firing rate begins to increase before GGN's membrane potential returns to baseline.
source: Notably, as evident in Figure 8b, IG's firing rate begins to increase before GGN's membrane potential returns to baseline.
evidence: This is an observation from the data shown in Figure 8b.

claim: IG's odor response cannot be driven solely by a reduction in inhibition from GGN.
source: This result rules out the possibility that IG's odor response is driven solely by a reduction in inhibition from GGN
evidence: This is a conclusion from the analysis of the data.

claim: IG receives odor-driven excitation from another pathway.
source: and suggests, rather, that IG receives odor-driven excitation from another pathway.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the analysis of the data.

claim: The model could reproduce realistic hyperpolarization in GGN's membrane potential by adding excitatory synapses to IG from either the KCs or the PNs.
source: Using our model, we could indeed reproduce realistic hyperpolarization in GGN's membrane potential by adding excitatory synapses to IG from either the KCs or the PNs (Figure 9a–e).
evidence: This is a result from the model simulation shown in Figure 9.

claim: Simulations produced a variety of membrane potential profiles in GGN including hyperpolarizations that varied with the odor-driven activity patterns in PNs.
source: Our simulations produced a variety of membrane potential profiles in GGN including hyperpolarizations; the profiles varied with the odor-driven activity patterns in PNs (Figure 9f–i).
evidence: This is a result from the model simulation shown in Figure 9.

claim: Spontaneous IPSPs in GGN persisted in preparations with silenced PNs and KCs.
source: We found that spontaneous IPSPs in GGN persisted in preparations with silenced PNs and KCs (Figure 9j, bottom red traces)
evidence: This is a result from in vivo recordings shown in Figure 9j.

claim: IG's spontaneous spiking either arises intrinsically or is driven by a source other than PNs or KCs.
source: demonstrating that IG's spontaneous spiking either arises intrinsically or is driven by a source other than PNs or KCs.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the in vivo recordings.

claim: It has been proposed that signals generated within GGN's α lobe branch propagate to its distant calyceal branch, where they provide global inhibition to all KCs.
source: It has been proposed that signals generated within GGN's α lobe branch propagate to its distant calyceal branch, where they provide global inhibition to all KCs (Papadopoulou et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from a previous study cited.

claim: Depolarizations of only about 2 mV in a non-spiking interneuron in the metathoracic ganglion of the locust can change the firing rate of its postsynaptic motor neuron.
source: For example, (Burrows and Siegler, 1978) showed that depolarizations of only about 2 mV in a non-spiking interneuron in the metathoracic ganglion of the locust can change the firing rate of its postsynaptic motor neuron.
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: Voltage steps from −50 mV to −45 mV in a graded synapse in the lobster stomatogastric ganglion can reliably evoke postsynaptic effects.
source: Similarly, (Manor et al., 1997) showed in a graded synapse in the lobster stomatogastric ganglion that voltage steps from −50 mV to −45 mV can reliably evoke postsynaptic effects.
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: GGN has the biophysical capacity to convey signals from KCs at GGN's α lobe branches to the calyx, providing effective global inhibition to all KCs.
source: Thus, we conclude that GGN has the biophysical capacity to convey signals from KCs at GGN's α lobe branches to the calyx, providing effective global inhibition to all KCs.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the model analysis.

claim: Imaging experiments in APL, the Drosophila analog of GGN, revealed different levels of Ca2+ activity in different spatial regions of its arbor when the animal was stimulated with low concentrations of odors.
source: Consistent with this, imaging experiments in APL, the Drosophila analog of GGN (Lin et al., 2014) revealed different levels of Ca2+ activity in different spatial regions of its arbor when the animal was stimulated with low concentrations of odors (Inada et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Some KCs are more effective than others at activating APL.
source: Inada et al. also found that some KCs are more effective than others at activating APL
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: APL provides diverse levels of inhibition to different subsets of KCs in the same brain.
source: and that APL, in turn, provides diverse levels of inhibition to different subsets of KCs in the same brain.
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: APL could provide local inhibition to a subset of KCs, likely through dendrodendritic connections between KCs and APL within the calyx.
source: By optogenetically activating a small subset of PNs, Inada et al. showed that APL could provide local inhibition to a subset of KCs, likely through dendrodendritic connections between KCs and APL within the calyx.
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: Reconstructions of APL based on serial section electron microscope images show that it receives synaptic connections from KCs throughout its arbor, including within the calyx.
source: Indeed, reconstructions of APL based on serial section electron microscope images show that it receives synaptic connections from KCs throughout its arbor, including within the calyx (Eichler et al., 2017; Zheng et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Strong odor stimuli appear to drive both GGN and APL to provide global inhibition to all KCs.
source: In vivo, strong odor stimuli appear to drive both GGN and APL to provide global inhibition to all KCs (Papadopoulou et al., 2011; Lin et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Depolarizations of GGN evoked by strong input can spread robustly throughout the giant neuron's arbor.
source: and our model shows (Figure 2) that depolarizations of GGN evoked by strong input can spread robustly throughout the giant neuron's arbor.
evidence: This is a result from the model shown in Figure 2.

claim: Blocking inhibitory inputs to KCs narrowed the dynamic range of their odor responses in Drosophila.
source: This prediction is consistent with observations made by imaging calcium in Drosophila where blocking inhibitory inputs to KCs narrowed the dynamic range of their odor responses (Inada et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: Examples of KCs that fire substantially more spikes, spontaneously and in response to odors, have been reported.
source: Although KCs generally respond very sparsely to any given odor, with very few cells firing just one or a few spikes (Laurent and Naraghi, 1994b; Perez-Orive et al., 2004; Mazor and Laurent, 2005), examples of KCs that fire substantially more spikes, spontaneously and in response to odors, have been reported (Perez-Orive et al., 2002; Gupta and Stopfer, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: It has been hypothesized that IG receives input from KCs.
source: It has been hypothesized that IG receives input from KCs (Papadopoulou et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from a previous study cited.

claim: KCs require strong and coincident input from PNs to spike.
source: Indeed, a version of our model in which all KCs synapse upon IG reliably reproduced fairly realistic odor-elicited hyperpolarizations in GGN. This result leads us to hypothesize that KCs, which require strong and coincident input from PNs to spike (Perez-Orive et al., 2002; Jortner et al., 2007)
